text: Growing your own vegetables is easier than most people think.
You do not need a big garden. A sunny balcony and a few large pots are enough to start.
Choose easy plants first, like tomatoes, chilies, spinach and mint.
Fill each pot with good soil mixed with compost and make sure there are holes at the bottom so extra water can drain away.
Plant the seeds about as deep as twice their size, then water them gently.
Most vegetables need at least five hours of direct sunlight every day so place the pots where the light is strongest.
Water in the early morning or the evening when the sun is not too hot.
Check the leaves every few days for insects and remove them by hand.
In a few weeks, you will see the first flowers and soon after, your first harvest.
Save a few seeds from your best plants for next season and share the extra harvest with your neighbors.
Gardening also teaches patience because every plant grows at its own pace.
There is nothing quite like eating a tomato you grew yourself.

How do solar panels turn sunlight into electricity? Let us take it step by step.
A solar panel is made of many small cells, usually built from material called silicon.
Silicon is a semiconductor, which means it can carry electricity under the right conditions.
When sunlight hits a solar cell, tiny particles of light called photons knock electrons loose from the silicon atoms.
The cell is built with two layers that push these free electrons in one direction.
That steady flow of electrons is an electric current.
Thin metal lines on the surface of the cell collect this current and send it out through wires. But there is a catch.
The electricity that comes out of a panel is direct current, while most homes use alternating current.
So a box called an inverter converts it into the kind of power your lights and fridge can use.
On a sunny day, a home system can produce more power than the family needs.
The extra power can charge a battery for the evening or flow back into the grid for neighbours to use.
Panels work best when they face the sun and are kept free of dust and shade.
Even on cloudy days, they still produce some power just less.
A typical panel keeps working for 25 years or more, with very little maintenance.
Today, solar power is one of the cheapest ways to produce electricity in many parts of the world.
From rooftops in busy cities to large solar farms in the desert, the same simple idea is at work.

On a small rocky island there was an old lighthouse and a keeper named Mara.
Every evening she climbed the 120 steps to light the great lamp. Most nights were quiet.
She watched the fishing boats come home and the gulls settle on the rocks, but one winter night a storm rolled in from the sea.
The wind howled and the waves crashed against the walls.
Suddenly the power went out and the lamp went dark.
Mara knew a ship was still out there in the rain.
She found an old oil lantern, lit it with shaking hands and held it high in the window.
For hours she stood there, refilling the oil and keeping the small flame alive.
At dawn the storm finally passed.
Far below a fishing boat sailed safely into the harbour.
The captain looked up and waved at the tiny light in the tower.
Mara smiled, blew out the lantern and went down the steps to make a hot cup of tea.
